body: **Summary:** Auto OEMs assemble and sell vehicles through dealer networks. Profit is volume times realisation minus commodity cost (steel, aluminium, precious metals), with operating leverage on high fixed costs. Key metrics: volume growth (wholesale against retail), market share, EBITDA margin, realisation per vehicle and mix (SUV and premium share), dealer inventory days, export share, EV share, and R&D/capex intensity. Cycle drivers: rural income and monsoon (2W, tractors), interest rates and financing availability, fuel prices, regulation cost-push (BS-VI 2020, OBD-II, safety norms), GST rates (the Sep 2025 cut to 18% on small cars and 2Ws under 350cc), the CV cycle tied to infrastructure and freight, and commodity prices. Lead indicators: Vahan daily registrations, FADA monthly retail, SIAM monthly wholesales, dealer inventory commentary, tractor sales, diesel consumption (PPAC), e-way bills, freight rates. Winners (Maruti 2003–17, Eicher 2010–17, TVS 2020–26, M&M SUVs 2021–26) hit a product cycle, gained share and expanded margins through premiumisation. Losers missed segment shifts (Hero in premium and scooters, Tata PV pre-2020) or overpaid for global assets. Valuation: P/E ~18–30x. The auto sector was ~24x in Oct 2026 against a 23x long-term average. CV makers should be valued on mid-cycle earnings. Nov 2026: Oct 2026 SIAM wholesales were PV 5.19 lakh (+12.4%) and 2W 25.8 lakh (+16.1%), but FADA retail fell (PV −14%, 2W −28%) because Diwali moved into November. Traps: confusing wholesale with retail, and a one-time GST pull-forward. Sources: [1](https://www.businesstoday.in/auto/story/auto-industry-posts-record-october-sales-as-passenger-vehicles-cross-5-lakh-mark-2-wheelers-grow-16-567320-2026-11-13) · [2](https://www.autocarpro.in/analysis-sales/passenger-vehicle-retail-sales-fall-1423-percent-to-508-lakh-in-october-fada-135776) · [3](https://plindia.com/ResReport/Quant-3-11-26-PL.pdf) Links: about `case_study:eicher-motors`

body:
`case_study:india-ipo-mania-2021` | confidence: **verified** | tags: india, blowup, ipo, rerating, sector-tech

2021 was a record IPO year - roughly $12-18bn raised depending on counting method; market cap/GDP reached ~115% (June 2021) and ~122% (Sept 2021), a 13-year high. Loss-making platform companies listed at rich valuations: Zomato (July 2021) and Nykaa (Nov 2021, +~80% on debut) surged on listing; Paytm (Nov 2021, issue price Rs 2,150, India's largest IPO then at ~$2.4-2.5bn) fell ~27% on debut. By mid-2022 Paytm was ~Rs 692 (-68% from issue), Zomato had lost ~66%, Nykaa ~50% from its high; five famed tech IPOs shed $18bn+ in value by Nov 2022. Paytm later fell further after the RBI's 2024 action against Paytm Payments Bank (to ~Rs 310-ish, ~-85%; from memory). Divergence: Zomato (now Eternal) later recovered far above its IPO price as quick commerce and food delivery turned profitable - the sector-wide crash was not uniform. Broad market: Nifty ~18,600 (Oct 2021) to ~15,200 (June 2022), ~-18% (from memory), as the Fed began tightening. Signals at the top: grey-market premiums, subscriptions in the tens-to-hundreds of times, valuation on GMV/'TAM' not profits, record new demat accounts and retail F&O growth, pre-IPO investors selling large OFS portions. Lesson: at IPO, the seller sets the price and the timing; wait for post-listing lock-up expiries and proof of unit economics.

body:
**False alarm (until the merger): HDFC Bank at 25-35x earnings and ~4x book** (`case_study:false-alarm-hdfc-bank-expensive-bank`, single-source). FLAG: a bank at trailing P/E 23-38 for most of 2005-2020 (median 26) and several times book, when most Indian banks traded at 1-2x book. CONTEXT: book-multiple is only 'expensive' relative to the ROE it earns and how long it can grow. HDFC Bank earned ROE 16-20% every year FY15-23 with low NPAs, a large low-cost CASA deposit base and ~20% loan growth, so book value compounded ~18-20% a year with no equity-destroying credit cycle; EPS rose 10.66 (FY15) -> 46.26 (FY25). Stock: ~Rs 28 (2005) -> ~Rs 1,000 (2026 peak), ~35x. WHERE IT TURNED: after the Jul-2023 merger with parent HDFC Ltd, ROE fell to ~14% and growth slowed as the bank had to raise deposits to replace HDFC's borrowings; P/E fell to ~16. From Jan 2021 (Rs 712) to Nov 2026 (Rs 824) the stock gained ~16% in ~6 years. LESSON: a premium P/B is justified by (ROE - cost of equity) x runway; when either input steps down (merger, slower growth), the premium compresses even without any credit problem. Contrast Yes Bank, whose similar-looking ROE was manufactured.

**False alarm (with luck): Apollo Hospitals' 76% promoter pledge** (`case_study:false-alarm-apollo-hospitals-promoter-pledge`, verified). FLAG: in 2019 the Reddy family had pledged ~68-78% of its holding (reports: 'likely to hit 75%', Jul 2019); the family sold a 3.6% stake to cut it, taking its holding to ~30.8%. Our hard rule (pledge >25% or rising) disqualifies this. CONTEXT: (1) the pledge was at the family level, the listed company itself was not over-levered and its core hospitals were profitable (OPM 10-15%, CFO Rs 537-1,293 cr FY18-20); (2) purpose and lenders were disclosed and management publicly committed to a reduction path (to ~20-25% by Nov 2019); (3) the trend was falling, funded by actual stake sales rather than promises; (4) the group had no history of fund diversion. By Aug 2025 a 1.3% block sale (Rs 1,489 cr) cut the pledge from 13.1% to ~2% of promoter holding. ROCE recovered from 7% (FY18) to 17%. Stock: ~Rs 1,293 (2019) -> Rs 9,040 (Nov 2026), ~7x. HONEST CAVEAT: a 2020-style crash could have triggered invocations; it worked partly because the price rose. LESSON: pledge severity depends on purpose, % of holding, trend, lender type, company leverage and group history; a high but falling, disclosed, family-level pledge with a clean group is a sizing/monitoring issue, not proof of fraud.
